Day 2, tick 226 (5:00am July 2): Both armies hold their positions overnight. Lee decides to make the principal attack on the Union left: Longstreet is to place McLaws's and Hood's divisions on the right of Hill's corps and drive in the Union left, Hill is to threaten the Union center, and Ewell is to make a demonstration on the Union right, to be converted into a real attack if opportunity offers. // Accounts of an argument between Lee and Longstreet over a flank movement come from postwar writings, not from the Official Records; Longstreet's own report says only that, with two divisions up, he delayed until Law's brigade rejoined about noon (OR 27/2 p.358).

Day 2, tick 254 (3:45pm): McLaws's division gets into position opposite the Union left about 4 p.m., and Hood's division is moved farther to the right, partly enveloping the Union left. Alexander's artillery battalion is posted to open on the Peach Orchard line.

Day 1, tick 38 (8:10am): The fighting on the pike dies down. Doubleday reforms the I Corps on McPherson's and Seminary Ridges; Howard arrives about 11:30 a.m. and takes command of the field as senior officer. Heth, whose division had been repulsed, rests his men in line for an hour or more before ordering the next attack with Pender's division in support. // The lull lasted until Ewell's corps appeared on the Union right in the early afternoon.

Day 3, tick 500 (8:05am): Pickett's three Virginia brigades (Garnett, Kemper, Armistead) form behind Seminary Ridge in the woods for the attack. Lee's report says they arrived near the field during the afternoon of July 2. // Contested: when Pickett's division reached the field (the afternoon of July 2 in Lee's report; about 9 a.m. July 3 in one timeline).

Day 1, tick 66 (10:30am): Schimmelfennig, cut off in the retreat through the town, hides within the enemy's lines and is still hidden days later; Colonel von Amsberg of the 45th New York takes the brigade. The I Corps' remnants fall back through the town.

Day 2, tick 298 (11:00am): SICKLES IS WOUNDED. A cannon shot takes off his right leg near the Trostle farm and he is carried from the field; Birney takes command of the III Corps. // The story that Sickles smoked a cigar as he was carried off is a tradition, not in the Official Records.

Day 1, tick 49 (9:05am): Carter's artillery battalion of Rodes's division fires from Oak Hill into the flank of the I Corps' right. Early's artillery (Jones's battalion), arriving on the Heidlersburg road, opens on the columns moving against Doles's left.

Day 1, tick 37 (8:05am): The 6th Wisconsin, 95th New York and 14th Brooklyn reach the edge of the Railroad Cut and the Confederates in it throw down their arms. Major John A. Blair surrenders the 2nd Mississippi; Major Hauser reports sending to the rear 7 officers and about 225 men. The 2nd Mississippi's battle flag, taken by Corporal F. Asbury Waller, is sent to army headquarters. The 6th Wisconsin loses at least 160 men killed or wounded in the charge.

Day 2, tick 340 (2:20pm): Fighting dies down across the field. The Confederates hold part of the XII Corps' works on the Union right; the Union line on Cemetery Ridge and Cemetery Hill is intact, and the III Corps has been driven back from its advanced line. // The Official Records give casualties for the whole battle, not for single days.

Day 1, tick 35 (7:55am): Davis's brigade presses Cutler's retiring regiments. Part of the 2nd and 42nd Mississippi shelter in the unfinished Railroad Cut north of the pike. Hall's battery, with no infantry left beside it, loses horses and a gun and falls back by sections along the railroad grading.

Day 3, tick 483 (7:20am): COLGROVE'S CHARGE. After about two hours of sharpshooter fire from daylight, with the firing on his left receding, Colonel Colgrove is told to advance; across the 100-yard open meadow in front of the Confederate breastworks he sends the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana at the double-quick. The 2nd Massachusetts loses about 130 and the 27th Indiana 112, the regiment commander Lieutenant Colonel Mudge among the killed; the 27th is called back behind the works and the Confederates' counter-charge is broken by the fire of the Union works. // Contested: the hour (Colgrove's report puts it about two hours after daylight; Williams says forenoon; others later). Mudge's reported last words, 'It is murder, but it is the order', come from survivors' later accounts, not the Official Records.

Day 1, tick 62 (10:10am): The I Corps' right on Oak Ridge is outflanked and enfiladed as Ewell's divisions press it. Paul, commanding Robinson's First Brigade, is severely wounded and command passes through Leonard, Root and Coulter. Robinson orders the 16th Maine alone to take a hill commanding the road and hold it as long as there was a man left; it loses 223 men and is forced back.
Day 2, tick 440 (7:20pm): Johnson's division holds the lower works it has taken. The XII Corps prepares to drive it out at daybreak.

Day 2, tick 252 (7:10am): About 3 p.m. Meade rides to the left, finds Sickles's corps in advance of the line designed for it, and is explaining that it is too far forward and discussing withdrawing it when the Confederate batteries open and infantry columns come on in a vigorous assault.
Day 2, tick 271 (8:45am): O'Rorke leads the 140th New York down the slope toward Devil's Den against the Texans and Alabamians pressing the hill, and is killed at the head of his regiment.

Day 1, tick 56 (9:40am): Early's division arrives by the Heidlersburg road. Early opens with artillery on the columns moving against Doles's left and orders Gordon's brigade in on Doles's left; after an obstinate contest Gordon breaks Barlow's division and captures General Barlow, who is severely wounded. Doles's brigade attacks north of the town.

Day 2, tick 302 (11:20am): THE 1ST MINNESOTA CHARGES. Hancock sees a Confederate column (Wilcox's brigade, in Fox's account) emerging near an unprotected part of his line and, wanting to gain time until reinforcements can come up, orders Colonel Colvill's 1st Minnesota to take the enemy's colors. The regiment charges, captures a color and forces the enemy back. // Hancock is reported to have said later that he saw he must gain five minutes' time; Hancock's own report says the regiment lost three-fourths of the officers and men engaged (OR 27/1 p.371). Fox gives 262 engaged and 224 casualties, nearly all in this fight (215 killed and wounded on July 2).

Day 1, tick 14 (6:10am): About three miles from Gettysburg Archer's brigade meets Buford's advance. Archer and Davis are thrown into line on either side of the pike and Pegram's artillery battalion comes into action from the ridge west of the Willoughby Run, while Buford's dismounted cavalry holds the ridges in front of the town.

Day 3, tick 523 (1:30pm): EAST CAVALRY FIELD. Stuart's cavalry (Hampton's, Fitzhugh Lee's and Chambliss's brigades) and Gregg's division with Custer's Michigan Brigade fight east of Gettysburg, on the Union right rear, while the infantry assault is made at the center. Lee's report says Stuart took position on Ewell's left and that the cavalry 'effectually protected our left'. // Contested: the hour the fight opened (about 1:00 to 2:30 p.m. in different accounts).

Day 1, tick 29 (7:25am): The Iron Brigade drives Archer's brigade back across the Willoughby Run. Brigadier General James J. Archer is captured, brought in by Private Patrick Maloney of Company G, 2nd Wisconsin, who is killed later in the day. Doubleday reports nearly 1,000 prisoners from Archer's brigade; Heth says Archer fell into the enemy's hands with some 60 or 70 of his men.

V-023 "Lee Meets His Men" (tick 556): As the survivors of the assault came back toward Seminary Ridge, Lee rode out to meet them. Lee's report says the troops were rallied and re-formed and the enemy did not pursue. The words reported from him, such as 'It is all my fault', come from witnesses' later accounts, among them Imboden's postwar article.

V-013 "Greene's Lone Stand" (tick 315): When most of the XII Corps was sent to the left on July 2, Greene's brigade of five New York regiments (74 officers and 1,350 men by Geary's count, 1,424 in all) held the entrenched Culp's Hill alone against Johnson's division, which attacked about two hours after the opening on the right; Greene was reinforced during the evening by detachments from the I and XI Corps.

V-006 "Gordon and Barlow" (tick 57): Gordon's brigade broke Barlow's division on the knoll north of Gettysburg and Barlow, severely wounded, was captured. The story that Gordon gave him water, promised to tell his wife, and years later met him as a friend comes from Gordon's own later account; some of its details have been questioned, and none is in the Official Records.

V-014 "The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill" (tick 326): At dusk on July 2 Hays's Louisiana brigade and Hoke's North Carolina brigade, under Colonel Avery, charged Cemetery Hill from the town. Lee's report says they drove two lines from the fences, forced their way into the works on the crest and seized several pieces of artillery, but a heavy force advanced against their unsupported right and they were compelled to retire, bringing out about 100 prisoners and four stand of colors.

V-018 "Cushing's Battery" (tick 553): Lieutenant Alonzo Cushing commanded Battery A, 4th U.S. Artillery (six 3-inch rifles) at the Angle. Webb reports that he fought for an hour and a half after reporting that he was wounded in both thighs, and was killed at the fence by the side of his guns; Hunt lists him among the battery commanders killed. He was awarded the Medal of Honor in 2014.

V-019 "Pickett's Return" (tick 557): After the repulse Pickett's division came back across the fields. The Confederate return counts 2,888 casualties in it, 1,499 of them captured or missing (OR 27/2 p.339); Lee reports that Armistead and Garnett were killed and Kemper dangerously wounded. Pickett's remark that he had no division is a tradition from later accounts.

V-022 "Mudge and the Charge at Culp's Hill" (tick 483): On the morning of July 3 Colonel Colgrove sent the 2nd Massachusetts and the 27th Indiana across the open meadow in front of the Confederate breastworks on Culp's Hill. The 2nd Massachusetts lost about 130 killed and wounded, including its commander, Lieutenant Colonel Mudge, and the 27th Indiana 112. The hour is disputed and Mudge's reported last words come from survivors' later accounts.

V-005 "Iverson's Pits" (tick 52): Iverson's North Carolina brigade attacked the stone wall on Oak Ridge held by Robinson's division, was struck by musketry from behind it, and lost heavily; Rodes wrote that its dead 'lay in a distinctly marked line of battle'. The Confederate return prints 820 casualties for the brigade, though its own rows add to 763.

V-010 "Chamberlain's Charge" (tick 275): At a crisis on the left of Little Round Top Colonel Chamberlain ordered the 20th Maine to the bayonet. The regiment swept down the hill and the Confederate front line threw down its arms. Chamberlain reported 400 prisoners, mainly from the 15th and 47th Alabama with some of the 4th and 5th Texas, and 150 of the enemy killed and wounded in front of his position; the hour of the charge is disputed.

V-021 "Farnsworth's Charge" (tick 568): About 5 p.m. on July 3 Kilpatrick ordered Farnsworth's brigade to charge on the Confederate right south of the Round Tops, and Farnsworth was killed leading it. Farnsworth had been a brigadier general since June 29. Reports that he protested, and the words said to have passed between him and Kilpatrick, come from survivors' later accounts.
McPherson's Ridge: First major defensive position July 1. Buford's dismounted cavalry then Reynolds's I Corps. Iron Brigade charged into Herbst Woods from this ridge. (elevation 570 ft)
Willoughby Run: Small stream at base of McPherson's Ridge. Iron Brigade crossed this charging into Herbst Woods.
Hagerstown Road: Confederate retreat route July 4-5. Anderson's division on this road.
Railroad Cut (unfinished railroad grade): Davis's brigade trapped here. 6th Wisconsin's famous charge. Unfinished cut too deep to escape quickly.
Culp's Hill: Union right flank anchor. XII Corps held against Johnson's division. Greene's lone stand July 2 night. Fighting from about dawn to about 11 a.m. on July 3. (elevation 640 ft)
Rose Woods: Fighting between Peach Orchard and Wheatfield. DeTrobriand's and Kershaw's brigades fought here. Stone wall along northern edge. (elevation 560 ft)
Lutheran Theological Seminary: Cupola used for observation. Perrin's charge broke through Seminary grounds July 1.
Carlisle Road: Led north from the town to Carlisle. Rodes's division came down the Middletown road to Oak Hill.

Tour stop 6 "Devil's Den" (The Triangular Field — July 2, 4:30 PM; tick 268): Below Little Round Top, the massive boulders of Devil's Den provided a natural fortress. Hood's Texas Brigade fought its way through the rocky terrain, driving Ward's Union brigade from the position. Confederate sharpshooters occupied the crevices among the boulders and fired on Little Round Top throughout the afternoon. The famous photograph of a Confederate sharpshooter dead among the rocks was later revealed to have been staged by photographer Alexander Gardner. The fighting in the triangular field between Devil's Den and the Wheatfield was some of the most confused and brutal of the entire battle.

Story marker "Hancock wounded here about 3:30 PM July 3 (Meade reports Hancock and Gibbon both severely wounded). His own dispatch says he was shot with a tenpenny nail and did not leave the field until the victory was secure" (tick 554)
Story marker "Lt. Cushing, wounded in both thighs, fought on here and was killed at the fence by his guns during the assault, about 3:30 PM July 3 (accounts 3:00 to 3:45)" (tick 548)
Story marker "Irish Brigade — Advanced into the Wheatfield; regimental tradition says the men wore sprigs of green boxwood in their caps" (tick 278)

Tour stop 11 "Cemetery Ridge" (Wright's Breakthrough — July 2, 7:30 PM; tick 315): In the fading light of July 2, Ambrose Wright's Georgia brigade achieved what no other Confederate force managed that day: Lee's report says Wright gained the crest of the ridge itself. Lee reports that Wright, having become separated from McLaws and gone beyond the other brigades of his division, was attacked in front and on both flanks and compelled to retire, unable to bring off any of the captured artillery. Hancock rushed every available man to seal the breach. The crisis passed. Whether the fight shaped Lee's decision to attack the center the next day is a matter of interpretation.

Story marker "Armistead fell here at Cushing's guns about 3:35 PM July 3 and was left mortally wounded within the Union lines (Harrow). Later accounts say he asked that a message and keepsake go to Hancock; that is tradition" (tick 551)

Tour stop 4 "Seminary Ridge" (The Union Retreat — July 1, 4:00 PM; tick 72): By mid-afternoon on July 1, the Union position north and west of Gettysburg had become untenable. The XI Corps was streaming back through the town in disorder, and the I Corps' right flank was exposed. The survivors rallied on Cemetery Hill south of town, where Howard had left Steinwehr's division as a reserve. The high ground — Cemetery Hill, Culp's Hill, and the long spine of Cemetery Ridge — would become the Union fishhook line that determined the battle's outcome. General Hancock arrived on Meade's order (3 p.m. by his own report, 4 p.m. by Howard's) and helped form the line. His 5:25 dispatch said the position on Cemetery Hill "cannot well be taken. Story marker "1st Minnesota — Charged Willcox's brigade on Hancock's order to gain time; Fox counts 224 casualties of 262 engaged for the battle (215 on July 2), the highest percentage of any Union regiment in a single battle in his tables" (tick 295)

Tour stop 8 "Peach Orchard" (Sickles' Salient Falls — July 2, 6:00 PM; tick 278): General Daniel Sickles, the controversial III Corps commander, advanced his corps some half a mile to three-quarters of a mile forward of the line assigned to it on Cemetery Ridge (Meade's estimate) to the higher ground around the Peach Orchard. The move created a vulnerable salient with exposed flanks on both sides. Barksdale's Mississippi brigade charged the Peach Orchard and Barksdale was mortally wounded in the attack. The assault swept through the orchard and broke the III Corps' advanced line. Sickles himself was struck by a cannonball that mangled his leg. He was carried from the field smoking a cigar, reportedly to reassure his men. His leg was amputated; he later donated it to the A

Whether Sickles's advance was authorized is disputed (Meade's report says he did not fully apprehend his instructions).
